q: What is the aim of optical character recognition as chapter 22 uses it?
options: To make a scanned image sharper so that a person reads it more easily
To turn the text in an image into a string that string methods and regular expressions can work on
To store an image inside a text file as a long string of characters
To translate the words of an image into another language
why: OCR extracts the text from an image so that a program can then apply string methods and regular expressions to it.

q: Which parts do the four lines of the chapter use to read text from an image?
options: The Tesseract engine, the NAPS2 application, the PyAutoGUI screenshot and OCRmyPDF
Pillow, a language model, a spellchecker and a PDF reader
PyTesseract, the subprocess module, NAPS2 and a scanner
The idea of OCR, the Tesseract engine, the PyTesseract package and Pillow
why: OCR, the Tesseract engine, PyTesseract and Pillow are the four parts that the four lines use.

q: Which kind of image does Tesseract suit best?
options: A photograph of a street scene with signs in it
A printed document with clear text
A page of handwriting written with a pen
A drawing without any letters on it
why: Tesseract is meant for printed documents; scene photographs and handwriting are not its task.

q: Where is the Tesseract engine installed?
options: Inside Python, with the pip command alone
On the computer, outside Python, with the system's own installer or package manager
Inside the Pillow package, which carries a copy
In the PyTesseract package, which bundles it
why: The engine is a separate program installed on the computer; Python only starts it and reads what it returns.

q: Why is installing PyTesseract with pip not enough to read an image?
options: PyTesseract needs a screen to display the image first
The tesseract program that does the recognition must also be installed on the computer
Pillow must be replaced by a newer image package
Python must be told the language of the image in the install command
why: PyTesseract only calls the separate tesseract program, so that program has to exist on the computer.

q: What does the section on reading text cover?
options: The installation of the engine on three systems
The steps of a NAPS2 command line
The correction of text by a language model
The four lines that read an image, and the further outputs PyTesseract offers
why: Reading text takes four lines, and PyTesseract offers more outputs than the chapter shows.

q: Roughly how much code does the basic reading program need?
options: About forty lines because each letter is handled in its own loop
One line, because PyTesseract opens files by itself without imports
About four hundred lines to train the engine on the font
About four lines: two imports, an image opened and a call that returns the text
why: The chapter shows the whole basic program in four lines: imports, Image.open() and image_to_string().

q: What do the other outputs of PyTesseract add to plain text?
options: A table of words with boxes and confidences, and a searchable PDF
A spoken version of the words and their translation
A scanned copy of the image in black and white only
A list of all fonts found in the image
why: image_to_data() gives a word table, and a PDF with the text under the image can be returned as well.

q: Why does the chapter discuss image quality?
options: Because Tesseract refuses images smaller than a fixed size
Because quality is the only thing that changes the speed
Because Pillow cannot open an image of poor quality
Because the quality of the image decides how good the recognised text is
why: A cleaner image with dark level text on a light background gives better text than a poor one.

q: What do the flaws of recognised text have in common?
options: They are only caused by a wrong language setting
They always make the program stop with an exception
They are mistakes that stay in the result, so the text is a draft to be checked
They appear only when the image is in colour
why: Hyphens, confused characters, mixed columns and wrong numbers all remain in the returned text.

q: What does input preparation try to improve?
options: The text returned by Tesseract, after it has been read
The speed of the Python interpreter that runs the program
The image given to Tesseract, before the engine reads it
The size of the language pack file that is installed
why: Cropping, inverting, straightening, bordering, thresholding and denoising all change the image, not the text.

q: What is the problem the correction section deals with?
options: Mistakes in the way the engine is installed
Mistakes in the name of the language pack
Mistakes in the recognised text that the engine has already made
Mistakes in the image file format
why: After reading, the text may still hold errors, and the section looks at machine ways to repair and check it.

q: Which kind of help does the section on machine fixes describe?
options: Programs and models that try to repair the recognised text
Programs that make the scan sharper before reading
Programs that install the engine on each computer
Programs that print the text on paper
why: Spellchecking, hyphen joining and a language model are the machine ways to repair the text.

q: What is the purpose of the checking section?
options: To prove that the recognised text has no errors at all
To stop the program when the first error is found
To show a reviewer where the correction changed the text and by how much
To compare the image with a second image
why: Review by difference and a similarity ratio tell a person where to look closely.

q: What does the languages section explain?
options: How Python translates one language to another
How the interface of Tesseract is shown in other languages
How Tesseract is told which language, or languages, the text is written in
How the program names are written in other alphabets
why: Language packs and the lang argument decide which letters and words Tesseract expects.

q: What is a language pack?
options: A Python module that translates the recognised text
A folder of images used to train the user
A data file of the engine for one language, installed apart from the engine
A setting of PyTesseract that is saved in the registry
why: A language pack is a .traineddata file named after its language code.

q: What does choosing a language mean in a program?
options: Changing the language in which the error messages are shown
Passing the lang argument so that the engine uses the right pack
Selecting the language of the operating system
Choosing the language of the Python documentation
why: The lang argument names the pack; left out it means English.

q: What does the NAPS2 section teach?
options: How to write a new OCR engine in Python
How to combine images into a searchable PDF by starting NAPS2 from Python
How to scan a paper page with PyAutoGUI
How to install Tesseract from the NAPS2 window
why: NAPS2 has a command-line form that Python starts with subprocess.run().

q: What kind of thing is NAPS2 in relation to Python?
options: A Python package that is imported with import
A separate scanning application that Python starts as a program
A Python function that is built in
A file format for scanned pages

Which folder the program is installed in

A program that gets its text from a screenshot of what is shown on the screen
A program that copies files between computers

q: What does the abbreviation OCR stand for?
options: Optical character recognition
Online content retrieval
Optimised code runner
Object classification and ranking
why: OCR is optical character recognition, the extraction of text from an image.

q: How does a Python script use the Tesseract engine?
options: It starts the separate program and reads what the program returns
It imports the engine as a Python module and calls its functions directly
It compiles the engine into the script at install time

options: NumPy
